title: Head-to-head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes (Shared‑Candidate Paired Design)
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that compares two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run used gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for end‑to‑end correctness (syntax, workflow constraints, and emulator reachability/isolation). Critically, the preregistration specified shared_initial_candidate semantics so both arms received the same LLM candidate per task. The confirmatory paired design executed 120 task pairs (240 episodes planned) with a single shared generation per pair (model_calls_used = 120). All completed episodes passed the deterministic validator in both arms (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because the design intentionally removed independent generation variance and no repairs were applied (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces), the run demonstrates validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than an independent head‑to‑head comparison of generation or repair robustness. We explicitly report these artifact‑grounded facts, add statistical caveats for the degenerate paired outcome, and recommend minimal preregistered changes required to discriminate architectures in follow‑up studies.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation and change sequencing with generative models promises operational efficiency but raises safety and correctness concerns. Architectures differ: translator→verifier toolchains seek constrained, formally checked outputs; agentic LLM pipelines iteratively generate, validate, and repair proposals. We asked: for intent‑driven changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and emulated topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (reachability and policy isolation): (A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? We preregistered a paired design (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) and executed it under an explicit shared_initial_candidate semantics so both arms received the identical LLM candidate per task. Contributions. (i) A complete, machine‑readable preregistered paired experiment executed on 120 task pairs using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic NetOps validator; (ii) artifact‑grounded confirmatory results and a precise statistical caveat for the degenerate paired outcome (n10 = n01 = 0); (iii) an explicit, minimal set of recommended preregistered changes (independent generation, per‑arm budgets, validator variability, hardware fidelity) needed to discriminate architectures.
sections.related_work: Prior work divides roughly into (i) formal translation and verification of configurations, which offers strong guarantees when device models exist, and (ii) LLM‑based NetOps and agentic systems that emphasize generation, self‑correction, and guardrails. Recent surveys and tutorials catalog agentic NetOps architectures and the need for validators and rollback contracts. Empirical comparisons exist but rarely combine preregistration, deterministic validators, and paired designs that isolate downstream acceptance behavior; our study situates itself to fill that narrowly defined experimental gap.
sections.methodology: Preregistration. The design was preregistered (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) and frozen prior to observing outcomes. Primary estimand: paired difference in binary end‑to‑end operational correctness (A − B) across n=120 paired intent tasks balanced by vendor×topology clusters. Key implementation choices (artifact‑grounded): generation model declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini; validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; execution adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Crucial preregistered semantic: shared_initial_candidate — both arms received the same single LLM candidate per pair (this choice was implemented and recorded in provider traces). Execution contract constrained one initial generation call per pair and allowed one repair iteration per task if triggered; actual execution used a single shared generation per pair (model_calls_used = 120). Outcome definition. End‑to‑end correctness is binary: validator acceptance of the final configuration after workflow/sequence and reachability checks. Analysis. Primary analysis used paired bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) and an exact McNemar two‑sided test executed by the archived paired_binary_analysis_v1. Statistical caveat (degenerate paired outcome). When discordant counts are zero (n10 = n01 = 0) the observed paired differences are constant; consequently (a) the paired bootstrap reproduces a degenerate sampling distribution equal to the observed constant difference and yields a point CI identical to that constant (here [0.00, 0.00] for 10,000 resamples, seed 1729), and (b) exact McNemar returns p = 1.0 because there are no discordant pairs to drive a paired preference. We report these artifact‑verified numbers and interpret them as showing validator‑acceptance parity under the shared‑candidate design, not as evidence of independent architectural equivalence.
sections.results: Execution summary. The preregistered run completed successfully (planned episodes 240; completed episodes 240; failed episodes 0) and used 120 model calls due to shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared generation per pair). Primary outcome. Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline success = 120/120 (100.0%); Guarded success = 120/120 (100.0%). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00. Paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Repairs and secondary estimands. No repairs were applied in any archived episode—validator_trace.repair_applied = false for all per‑task scoring artifacts—so preregistered secondary estimands concerning repair coverage and iteration counts are uninformative for this execution. Representative artifact evidence. Per‑task validator traces record normalized final states, validation_before/after metadata, and repair_applied flags; these artifacts confirm that initial shared candidates satisfied validator constraints and that no repair loop executed. Deterministic reconciliation confirms provider_call_audit and stage_counts with a single shared_initial_generation stage executed 120 times.
sections.discussion: Interpretation. Under the precise preregistered constraints—shared_initial_candidate generation, a single hosted LLM generation per pair, and a constraining deterministic validator—the two architectures produced validator‑satisfying outputs for every included task. The experiment therefore demonstrates parity in validator acceptance of identical candidates, not an independent head‑to‑head comparison of generator robustness or repair efficacy. Threats to validity and limits. Shared_candidate semantics intentionally remove generation variance (construct validity); emulator execution and synthetic tasks limit external validity; single LLM and single validator choices limit generality. The degeneracy of the paired outcome (n10 = n01 = 0) creates a ceiling effect: statistical tests and CIs are degenerate and must be interpreted as documenting observed parity under the chosen design rather than discriminating architectures. Minimal follow‑up design changes to discriminate architectures. To test intrinsic architectural differences we recommend preregistered changes: (i) independent generation per arm (remove shared_initial_candidate), (ii) per‑arm model and repair budgets, (iii) multiple LLMs and varying validator strictness, and (iv) higher‑fidelity device images or hardware evaluation. These changes were anticipated in the preregistration as follow‑up options.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired comparison of translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines across 120 intent task pairs using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic NetOps validator. Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and deterministic validation, both pipelines produced validator‑satisfying configurations for all tasks (100% each), yielding a paired difference of 0.00 (95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). Artifact traces show only a single shared LLM generation per pair and no repair activity; therefore, the run measured validator acceptance of identical candidates rather than independent architectural robustness. We present these artifact‑backed facts, add explicit statistical caveats for the degenerate paired outcome, and recommend precise preregistered changes necessary to produce a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison in future work.

limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics were preregistered and used; this intentionally removes variance from the generation stage and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.
Task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
Single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied=false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

Deterministic validator decisions can mask differences in explanation quality, human‑readability, or operator‑facing properties that matter in practice but were outside the binary end‑to‑end correctness metric used here.
